```{python}
span_max  = f"{cv_span['cv_rmse'].max():.3f}"
K1_rmse   = f"{cv_K.set_index('K').loc[1,'cv_rmse']:.3f}"
K2_rmse   = f"{cv_K.set_index('K').loc[2,'cv_rmse']:.3f}"
IS_SYNTH  = R["source"] != "open-meteo"

def md(text):  # emit a paragraph of Markdown with run-derived numbers baked in
    print(text)
```

## What a "normal" is, and the one decision that matters

Ask what a *normal* July day looks like in Germany and you are really asking a
statistical question: across many past years, what was the typical temperature on
that calendar day? Take the daily mean temperature for, say, the 7th of July in
every year from 1961 to 1990 and average it, and you have a normal for one day.
Do it for all 366 calendar days and you have a daily climatological reference — a
smooth seasonal curve that says what the year "should" feel like, against which
any individual year can be read.

The catch is *smooth*. With only thirty baseline years, each calendar day's
average still carries a lot of sampling noise: the raw day-of-year means jitter
up and down by a degree or more from one day to the next purely by chance, even
though the real seasonal march is gradual. So a daily normal has to be smoothed.
Too little smoothing and the reference line chases noise; too much and it flattens
out real features of the annual cycle. **How much to smooth is the single most
consequential choice in the whole exercise**, and the bulk of this article is
about making that choice with cross-validation rather than by eye — and, crucially,
re-deriving it for Germany rather than borrowing the value the Spanish original
landed on.

A second, deliberate choice: we keep the **1961–1990** reference period rather than
the WMO's current operational 1991–2020 normals. 1961–1990 predates most of the
recent warming, so it gives us a stable yardstick against which the change is
visible. If we updated the baseline to 1991–2020 we would be quietly folding the
warming into the reference line and measuring 2025 against an already-warmed
world.

## The data: ERA5 reanalysis via Open-Meteo

The temperatures come from the [Open-Meteo Historical Archive
API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api), which serves **ERA5
reanalysis** from the ECMWF — free, no API key. Reanalysis matters here: unlike
station records, it is spatially complete and gap-free, so a 1961–1990 baseline
never has to cope with a station that opened in 1975 or moved in 1983. For each
city we make a single archive call,

```text
https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive
    ?latitude=..&longitude=..
    &start_date=1961-01-01&end_date=1990-12-31
    &daily=temperature_2m_mean&timezone=auto
```

plus the same call for 2025, and cache every response to `data/*.parquet` with
exponential-backoff retries for rate limits. The fetch layer
(`german_normals.fetch`) never fabricates anything; in a sandbox where the host is
blocked it simply hands off to the synthetic generator, and the data source is
recorded and printed on every figure so there is no ambiguity about which you are
looking at.

## Where people live, not where the land is

Germany is climatically diverse but, unlike Spain, it is a single contiguous
domain — there are no Canary Islands to carve off. The sampling choice that *does*
carry over from the original is **population weighting**. We are not trying to
characterise the average German *hectare*; we want the temperature experienced by
the average German *resident*. So the city list is weighted toward where people
actually live.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cities
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The population-weighted sample: marker area is proportional to city population. The Rhine/Ruhr conurbation in the west pulls hard, as do Berlin, Hamburg and Munich."
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 5.4
import geopandas as gpd
cities = P["cities"]
germany = gpd.read_file(DATA / "germany.geojson")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 5.4))
germany.plot(ax=ax, color="#f4f4f4", zorder=0)
germany.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="#666", lw=0.8)
ax.scatter(cities["lon"], cities["lat"],
           s=8 + 90 * cities["population"] / cities["population"].max(),
           c="#c5462a", edgecolor="white", lw=0.4, alpha=0.85, zorder=3)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```

## The day-of-year band

Before smoothing, it is worth seeing the raw material. For each of the 366
calendar slots we take the distribution of the national daily mean across the
thirty baseline years and record its **median** and its **5th and 95th
percentiles**. A subtlety handled in code: leap years. Dates are projected onto a
fixed leap-reference calendar so that 1 March is always day 61 and 31 December is
always day 366; the only under-sampled slot is 29 February (day 60), populated by
the seven leap years in 1961–1990 alone.

```{python}
#| label: fig-band
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Raw day-of-year statistics of the population-weighted national mean over 1961–1990: median (line) and the 5th–95th percentile band. The band is visibly wider in winter — German winter weather is far more variable day-to-day than its summer."
clim = P["climatology"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.2))
ax.fill_between(clim["doy"], clim["p5"], clim["p95"], color="#9aa0a6", alpha=0.25)
ax.plot(clim["doy"], clim["median"], color="#2b2b2b", lw=1.6)
ax.set_xlim(1, 366); ax.set_ylabel("°C")
ax.set_xticks([1,32,61,92,122,153,183,214,245,275,306,336])
ax.set_xticklabels(["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"])
for s in (32,61,92,122,153,183,214,245,275,306,336):
    ax.axvline(s, color="#eee", lw=0.6)
for sp in ("top","right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

That winter-wide, summer-narrow band is the first genuinely German feature of the
picture, and it matters later: because the summer band is tight, it takes only a
modest warm anomaly for a 2025 summer day to punch through the 95th percentile.

## How smooth should the normal be? Cross-validation, by year

The median curve above is still too noisy to use as a reference. We smooth it two
ways and let the data choose the amount of smoothing in each.

The first is **loess** (local regression). Its `span` parameter sets the fraction
of the data inside each local window: small spans follow every wiggle, large spans
flatten the curve. We use `skmisc.loess` specifically because — unlike
statsmodels' LOWESS — it can *predict on new day-of-year points*, which is exactly
what cross-validation requires.

And the cross-validation must be split **by year, not by row**. A normal is a
statement about an unseen year, so we hold out whole calendar years: fit the loess
on the day-of-year/temperature pairs from four-fifths of the baseline years,
predict the held-out years' daily temperatures, and score the error. Splitting
randomly across rows would let the same warm summer leak into both train and test
and would flatter the tighter spans. We sweep a grid of spans through 5-fold
leave-years-out CV and take the minimum.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cv-span
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Leave-years-out CV RMSE against loess span. The curve is shallow — daily weather noise dominates the absolute error — but it has a clear, reproducible minimum."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.8))
ax.plot(cv_span["span"], cv_span["cv_rmse"], "-o", color="#2a5bc5")
best = cv_span.loc[cv_span["cv_rmse"].idxmin()]
ax.scatter([best["span"]], [best["cv_rmse"]], s=120, color="#c5462a", zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f"  best span = {best['span']:g}", (best["span"], best["cv_rmse"]),
            color="#c5462a", va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("loess span"); ax.set_ylabel("CV RMSE (°C)")
for sp in ("top","right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
md(
    f"For Germany the cross-validation picks a span of **{span_str}**. That is worth "
    f"dwelling on, because it is **not** the Spanish study's value (0.16) — and we "
    f"did not assume it would be. A larger span means *more* smoothing. The reason is "
    f"geographic: Germany's annual temperature cycle is flatter-topped and more "
    f"nearly symmetric than the Iberian one, without the sharp Mediterranean features "
    f"that reward a tighter, more flexible fit. With less fine structure to preserve, "
    f"the data are happy to be smoothed harder, and CV says so on its own.\n\n"
    f"A caveat the numbers make honest: the CV RMSE barely moves across the grid "
    f"(from about {span_max} °C down to {span_min} °C). That is expected and not a "
    f"failure — the absolute error is dominated by irreducible day-to-day weather "
    f"noise that *no* normal can predict. Cross-validation is not claiming the normal "
    f"explains the weather; it is only locating the smoothing level that generalises "
    f"best to unseen years, and that optimum is shallow but stable."
)
```

## The harmonic alternative, and how many harmonics Germany needs

The second method writes the annual cycle as a sum of sine/cosine pairs — a
**harmonic regression** with `K` harmonics over day-of-year, fitted by ordinary
least squares. `K = 1` is a single sinusoid (one warm peak, one cold trough);
each extra harmonic adds finer seasonal shape. We choose `K` with the same
leave-years-out CV.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cv-k
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "CV RMSE against harmonic order K. The jump from K=1 to K=2 is decisive; beyond that there is essentially nothing left to gain."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.8))
ax.plot(cv_K["K"], cv_K["cv_rmse"], "-o", color="#2a5bc5")
bk = cv_K.loc[cv_K["cv_rmse"].idxmin()]
ax.scatter([bk["K"]], [bk["cv_rmse"]], s=120, color="#c5462a", zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f"  best K = {int(bk['K'])}", (bk["K"], bk["cv_rmse"]), color="#c5462a", va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("number of harmonics K"); ax.set_ylabel("CV RMSE (°C)")
ax.set_xticks(cv_K["K"])
for sp in ("top","right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
md(
    f"Germany's optimum is **K = {K_str}** — again *lower* than the Spanish study's "
    f"K = 4, and again for a physical reason. A single harmonic ({K1_rmse} °C) is "
    f"clearly too rigid; the big improvement comes at K = 2 ({K2_rmse} °C), which "
    f"buys the asymmetry between a fast spring warm-up and a slower autumn "
    f"cool-down. Spain needs a fourth harmonic largely to capture the Mediterranean's "
    f"thermal inertia — the sea keeps coastal autumns warm well into the year, "
    f"bending the curve in a way a low-order fit cannot follow. Germany has no "
    f"comparable ocean-inertia autumn lag: the maritime northwest mildens winters and "
    f"cools summers (it narrows the *amplitude*) but does not add a sharp seasonal "
    f"kink, while the continental east is close to a clean sinusoid. So a lower K "
    f"suffices, exactly as the climate geography would predict.\n\n"
    f"Reassuringly, the two independently-chosen normals — loess at span {span_str} "
    f"and the K = {K_str} harmonic — agree to within **{gap_str} °C** across the "
    f"entire year. When two different smoothers, each tuned by cross-validation, land "
    f"on essentially the same curve, the reference itself is robust."
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-normals
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The two cross-validated normals overlaid. They are nearly indistinguishable — evidence the seasonal reference is not an artefact of one smoothing method."
nm = P["normals"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.plot(nm["doy"], nm["loess"], color="#2b2b2b", lw=2.2, label=f"loess (span {span_str})")
ax.plot(nm["doy"], nm["harmonic"], color="#c5462a", lw=1.4, ls="--", label=f"harmonic (K={K_str})")
ax.set_xlim(1, 366); ax.set_ylabel("°C"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_xticks([1,32,61,92,122,153,183,214,245,275,306,336])
ax.set_xticklabels(["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"])
for sp in ("top","right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

We use the loess curve as the reference line in what follows; the harmonic fit
would give the same story.

## 2025 against the normal

Now the payoff. We lay 2025's daily national mean over the 1961–1990 loess normal
and shade the difference: salmon where the year ran above normal, blue where below,
with darker fills wherever a day broke clean out of the 5th–95th percentile band.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fanchart
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Germany 2025 daily mean temperature against the 1961–1990 normal. Salmon = above normal, blue = below; darker fills mark days outside the historical P5–P95 band; circles flag each month's single most extreme day. Map inset shows the population-weighted city sample."
from IPython.display import Image
path = figure.make_fan_chart(P["comparison"], P["normals"], P["climatology"],
                             P["cities"], R, geojson_path=DATA / "germany.geojson",
                             out_path=FIG / "fan_chart.png")
Image(filename=str(path))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
md(
    f"Read against its own 1961–1990 baseline, 2025 was a **warm year almost "
    f"everywhere on the calendar**. Its national daily mean averaged **{mean25} °C** "
    f"against a normal of **{meannorm} °C**, an anomaly of **{anom_str} °C**; "
    f"**{warmshare}%** of all days landed above the normal line. The year cleared the "
    f"historical **95th percentile on {above95} days** — concentrated, as the tight "
    f"summer band foretold, in the warm season — and dropped below the **5th "
    f"percentile on only {below5} days**. The blue excursions that remain are the "
    f"exceptions that make the warmth legible: a genuine cold snap can still briefly "
    f"undercut a baseline that is now, on average, well below the present climate.\n\n"
    f"That asymmetry — many days above the upper edge, very few below the lower one — "
    f"is the fingerprint of a shifted distribution. Against a stationary 1961–1990 "
    f"world, roughly 5% of days *should* sit above the 95th percentile by "
    f"construction; 2025 put far more there. The reference line did its job precisely "
    f"because we refused to update it: held at 1961–1990, it lets the change show."
)
```

## Reproducing this with real data

Everything here is driven by one function. From the project root:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python run_analysis.py --fresh     # build data, cross-validate, cache products
quarto render article.qmd          # rebuild this page
```

```{python}

    f"answers, it fetches and caches real ERA5 for all {n_cities} cities and the "
    f"entire article rebuilds with genuine numbers and the data source on every "
    f"figure flips to *Open-Meteo ERA5*. Only when the host is unreachable does it "
    f"fall back to the labelled synthetic generator used for this render. The pure "
    f"functions — day-of-year indexing, weighted aggregation, the harmonic design "
    f"matrix and the by-year CV folds — are covered by `pytest` unit tests written "
    f"test-first; run `pytest -q` to see them pass."
)

md(
    f"\n::: {{.callout-note title=\"Method, in one paragraph\"}}\n"
    f"Pull ERA5 daily mean temperature for {n_cities} population-weighted German "
    f"cities (1961–1990 and 2025) from Open-Meteo; collapse the cities into one "
    f"population-weighted national daily series; for each of 366 calendar days take "
    f"the median and 5th/95th percentiles over the baseline; smooth the seasonal "
    f"normal with loess and with harmonic regression, choosing the loess span "
    f"(**{span_str}**) and harmonic order (**K = {K_str}**) by 5-fold cross-validation "
    f"split by year; then read 2025's daily anomalies and band exceedances against "
```
